claims.claim: Baur says the expected arc of play should be stated explicitly to players rather than kept coy.
claims.source: Wolfgang Baur, Kobold Press world building seminar transcript, part 2, 2025
claims.quote: you should be explicit about it. Don’t be coy

claims.claim: Noonan reports that a DM reading boxed text holds player attention for two sentences and no further.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, 'Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast, 2005
claims.quote: If you’re the DM, you get two sentences. Period.

claims.claim: Noonan's hypothesis was that boxed text longer than a paragraph probably is not worth reading aloud.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, 'Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast, 2005
claims.quote: boxed text longer than a paragraph probably isn’t worth reading

claims.claim: Noonan observed players repeatedly missing the actual data inside the boxed text, such as room dimensions and exits.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, 'Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast, 2005
claims.quote: players were missing the actual data in the boxed text

claims.claim: Noonan concludes that oration is inherently harder to concentrate on than conversation.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, 'Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast, 2005
claims.quote: oration is inherently harder to concentrate on than conversation

claims.claim: Noonan notes DMs are by and large reading the boxed text cold, from a script never uttered aloud before.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, 'Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast, 2005
claims.quote: DMs are, by and large, reading the boxed text cold

claims.claim: Writing in 2005, the authors say boxed text in adventures used to be a lot longer than it was then.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, 'Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast, 2005
claims.quote: used to be a lot longer than it is today
claims.page: 'Tangent Alert!' comparing Sons of Gruumsh with Return to the Keep on the Borderlands

claims.claim: The authors advise the DM to ditch boxed text and use his own words for the initial description of the room.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, 'Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast, 2005
claims.quote: use your own words for the initial description of the room

claims.claim: Dyson Logos dates boxed and read-aloud text to the 1e period of published adventures.
claims.source: Dyson Logos, 'The Dreaded Boxed Text', Dyson's Dodecahedron, 2013
claims.quote: During the 1e days, we saw the advent of “boxed” or “read-aloud” text

claims.claim: Dyson attributes boxed text to tournament use, whose goal was to standardize the experience for each play group.
claims.source: Dyson Logos, 'The Dreaded Boxed Text', Dyson's Dodecahedron, 2013
claims.quote: the goal being to standardize the game experience for each play group

claims.claim: Jara argues setting and rules frame the game because they invariably imply reductions of the imagined world.
claims.source: David Jara, 'Framings and Paratexts in Tabletop Role-playing Games', International Journal of Role-Playing 4, 2013

claims.claim: Jara treats the information a game setting gives as otherwise purely factual, to which intra-textual framing devices add diegetic meaning.
claims.source: David Jara, 'Framings and Paratexts in Tabletop Role-playing Games', International Journal of Role-Playing 4, 2013
claims.quote: factual information given by the game setting

claims.claim: Kim Mohan, D&D's longest-serving editor, praises Ed Greenwood's prose for leaving the reader feeling that fifty words are held back behind every word given.
claims.source: Kim Mohan, quoted by Ramanan Sivaranjan reporting the D&D podcast interview, 2013
claims.quote: you feel like he’s holding fifty in reserve

claims.claim: Mohan says that of every ten words Ed Greenwood supplies, three or four could probably have been kept back.
claims.source: Kim Mohan, quoted by Ramanan Sivaranjan reporting the D&D podcast interview, 2013
claims.quote: for every ten that he gives you he probably could

claims.claim: The D&D house style guide circulated to Guild creators is numbered version 1.08a and carries a 2018 Wizards of the Coast copyright line.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing v1.08a
